newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ SPORT-More sports violence may end up in court.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT-More sports violence may end up in court.

text.p: Changing attitudes to violence in sport could lead to more cases going to court, Hillary Commission for Fitness and Leisure spokesman John Boyd said on Tuesday.
The Hillary Commission is the government body responsible for sports funding and provides advice to the Government on sports policy.
Boyd told the New Zealand Press Association that court action against athletes "cannot be dismissed lightly -- as it might have been in the past, when the rough stuff was part of the game".
He said he was aware of legal action being taken by police against instances of sports violence in England, Scotland and Wales. Charges of grievous bodily harm had been brought.
"That's about as bad as an assault can get. We're talking very serious stuff there and our laws are basically the same."
Boyd said it was incongruous a punch witnessed by thousands on television could escape legal action, when a punch in the street would be brought before the courts, even if there was only one witness.
He said sports bodies must have approved systems of punishing violent offenders "otherwise the public will find it unacceptable".
He said there was also a legal issue related to player safety. Players had the right to expect protection from violence.
"You don't sign away all your civil rights when you walk on the playing field."
Boyd said he was not targeting any particular sport, or Waikato Chiefs rugby prop Richard Loe -- who was last night suspended for three weeks by a NZ Rugby Football Union judicial hearing.
Loe was banned for punching incidents during Saturday night's Super 12 game between Waikato and the Auckland Blues.
The issue of laying criminal charges for sports field violence was raised in June 1995 after violent play in Auckland college rugby matches.
At that time Auckland Secondary School Heads' Association chairman Hugh Richards said laying criminal charges was an appropriate response to violent play.
He issued the advice after a member of an Auckland college First 15 was kicked in the head by an opposing player during a secondary school rugby match.
The incident resulted in an injured player from St Peters College, Epsom, laying an assault complaint with police against a player from Nga Tapuwae College, south Auckland.
The incident left the St Peters College student unconscious.

Last April All Black Ian Jones was acquitted of an on-field assault after being found not guilty of deliberately kicking flanker Junior Paramore in the head during a match against Counties in Pukekohe in September 1995.
His barrister, Paul Davison, said he believed matters arising from the rugby field should be dealt with through the sporting body's internal disciplinary procedures.
At the same time, society had a right to ensure that criminal acts on the field of play should be subject to sanction by the courts.
